Week 12: Synthesis — Transformations in a Broken World

Governance & Methods
Lecture
Course synthesis: What have we learned? What remains unresolved? Reflection, celebration, and next steps.

Week 12 Synthesis Lecture + Discussion · 90 min

Synthesis — Transformations in a Broken World

Overview

The closing session revisits the opening question — why transformation? — from the vantage point of 12 weeks of frameworks, cases, and conversations. It does not provide closure but deepens the question: what does it mean to work for sustainability transformation in contexts of deep uncertainty, power asymmetry, and uneven vulnerability? The session ends with a forward-looking discussion on students’ own agency.

Learning Objectives

  1. Synthesise course frameworks into a coherent personal analytical toolkit.
  2. Reflect critically on the limits of academic knowledge for sustainability practice.
  3. Articulate what they will carry forward from the course into their own professional/civic life.

Topics Covered

1. Looking back (20 min)
Revisit the opening week’s provocation. What has changed? What has become more complex? Synthesis of key frameworks and their relationships.
2. What the frameworks miss (20 min)
Honest audit: Where did course frameworks fail to explain what we observed in cases and the field? Indigenous knowledge systems; affect, identity, and motivation; luck and contingency in transformation.
3. Agency in broken systems (20 min)
Individual vs. collective agency; “jamming the gears” vs. building alternatives; avoiding burnout and paralysis; the politics of hope (not optimism).
4. Final reflection circle (30 min)
Structured round: each student shares one thing they are taking forward and one unresolved question. Teaching team reflects back patterns they have observed across the cohort.

Assessment: Final Synthesis Essay

Due: Two weeks after the last session.

Prompt: Drawing on course frameworks and your case study, write an essay (2,000–2,500 words) that: 1. Analyses your case through at least three course frameworks 2. Reflects on the limits of these frameworks for your case 3. Identifies what you would need to know or do to support the transformation you studied

Evaluation: Framework depth (30%), critical reflection (30%), evidence (20%), communication (20%).

Localisation Note

For partner institutions

The “agency in broken systems” discussion lands very differently across contexts. In contexts of high vulnerability (e.g., communities experiencing active climate impacts), the discussion of hope and agency can feel hollow or even offensive if not handled carefully. We recommend grounding it in concrete examples of locally-led transformation before introducing theoretical frameworks about agency.

The final reflection circle is the most important ritual in the course. Protect its time — do not let logistics or essay instructions crowd it out. Students consistently report this as the most memorable part of the course.
